extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether a patent application’s specification sufficiently shows possession of the claimed invention under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description). Covers how to construe claims, review the specification, and apply tests for species/genus, means-plus-function, and biotechnology/chemical disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is an essential part of the examination process. Each claim must be separately analyzed and given its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description. The entire claim must be considered, including the preamble language and the transitional phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the preamble and transitional phrase in the analysis; determine whether preamble language constitutes a structural limitation. Treat transitional terms according to their established meanings: 'comprising' is open-ended (covers recited subject matter alone or in combination with unrecited subject matter); 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground but, absent clear specification, will be construed as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior art 102/103 searches. Do not import limitations into claims from the specification. Absence of definitions or details for well-established terms or procedures should not be the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112, first paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the entire application to assess support for claimed elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to determining whether the disclosure satisfies the written description requirement for the claimed subject matter, the examiner should review the claims and the entire specification, including the specific embodiments, figures, and sequence listings, to understand how applicant provides support for the various features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how applicant provides support for each element/step; an element may be critical where those skilled in the art would require it to determine possession. The review should determine the field of the invention and the level of skill/knowledge in the art, since these affect the specificity required. Rely on the specification (summary, detailed description), original claims, abstract, drawings, and sequence listings when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession may be shown by reduction to practice, detailed drawings, or identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention. Possession may also be shown by a clear depiction of the invention in detailed drawings or in structural chemical formulas which permit a person skilled in the art to clearly recognize that applicant had possession of the claimed invention. An adequate written description may be shown by any description of sufficient, relevant, identifying characteristics so long as a person skilled in the art would recognize that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: constructed embodiments or performed processes that meet all claim limitations (reduction to practice); detailed drawings; structural chemical formulas; deposits of biological materials per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. Identifying characteristics for biomolecules include sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length, restriction maps, etc. Functional descriptions coupled with known correlations between function and structure can suffice in some arts; function alone is inadequate where no such correlation exists. Case law examples cited (Pfaff, Cooper, Vas‑Cath, Eli Lilly, Enzo Biochem, Falkner, Capon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement for chemical and molecular inventions (precision required)
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate written description of a chemical invention requires a precise definition, such as by structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties, and not merely a wish or plan for obtaining the chemical invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely describing assays or screening methods without disclosing the actual compounds that achieve the claimed result is insufficient. For biological macromolecules, while examples are not always necessary, adequate characterization or identifying information (structure, sequence, deposit) is often required to show possession. Case examples: Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle; Noelle v. Lederman; Falkner v. Inglis; Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre-AIA 112, para. 6) written description test
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, para. 6, it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequacy under 35 U.S.C. 112(a)/pre-AIA 112, para. 1 for a means-/step-plus-function limitation is satisfied if: (1) the written description adequately links or associates adequately described particular structure, material, or acts to the function recited; or (2) it is clear based on the facts of the application that one skilled in the art would have known what structure, material, or acts perform the function. Consider the original disclosure in the summary, detailed description, original claims, abstract, and drawings. Note: a rejection under 112(a)/para. 2 cannot stand where there is adequate description in the specification regarding means-plus-function recitations that are not challenged for being unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species (single embodiment) vs genus claim analysis and checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limited to a single disclosed embodiment or species is analyzed as a claim drawn to a single embodiment or species; a claim that encompasses two or more embodiments/species is analyzed as a genus. For each claim drawn to a single embodiment/species, determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice, a reduction to drawings/structural formulas, or sufficiently detailed identifying characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the stepwise checklist: (A) Determine whether the application describes an actual reduction to practice of the claimed invention. (B) If not, determine whether the invention is complete as evidenced by reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed to show possession. (C) If not, determine whether the invention has been set forth in terms of distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficiently detailed to show possession. Then (1) ask whether the application describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole — if yes, written description satisfied; (2) if not, determine whether other relevant identifying characteristics (e.g., function coupled with known correlation to structure) would allow a skilled artisan to recognize possession. Disclosure of function alone, without correlation, is insufficient; compare arts where software or microprocessor disclosures may be adequate versus unpredictable biological arts where more detail is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in determining sufficiency of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows that applicant was in possession of the claimed invention is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include: level of skill and knowledge in the art at filing; partial structure; physical and/or chemical properties; functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known/disclosed correlation between structure and function; method of making the claimed invention. Patents and printed publications in the art should be relied upon to determine whether an art is mature and the level of knowledge/skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of maturity and predictability of the art on required disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with the scientific and technological knowledge already in existence. There is generally an inverse correlation between the level of skill/knowledge in the art and the specificity of disclosure necessary to satisfy the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mature technologies where knowledge/skill is high, written description questions should rarely be raised for originally filed claims even if the specification discloses only a method and function (example: microprocessors). In emerging, unpredictable, or less predictable technologies, more evidence/detail is required to show possession (examples: biological molecules where unpredictability demands structural detail rather than mere functional description). Use prior art to gauge maturity of the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base rejections on lack of detail for well-known information; applicant's burden when invoking limiting language
rubrics_metrics.description: Information which is well known in the art need not be described in detail in the specification. Conversely, if an applicant contends that additional steps/materials in the prior art are excluded by a recitation like 'consisting essentially of,' the applicant has the burden of showing that the introduction of additional steps/components would materially change the characteristics of applicant’s invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess what is conventional or well known in the art (citing Hybritech and related cases). Where applicant uses intermediate claim language ('consisting essentially of'), absent clear specification of what materially changes the invention, treat it as open for prior art purposes. Applicant must provide evidence/specification detail to justify narrower construction.
